blogs.title: Screenwriters, This Is the Audience Hollywood Isn’t Writing For
blogs.description:
Everyone in Hollywood is always looking for the next big idea that will strike oil and serve as a bellwether for the vague notion of "what people want to watch." Earlier this year, the relatively low-budget horror Obsession shook things up. Writer/director Curry Barker came from YouTube, so to YouTube everyone went in search of "the next one."

You've probably seen a slew of recently greenlit projects trying to capitalize on Internet horror. For instance, a "Jeff the Killer" movie is in development from Savanah Moss, a TikTok creator with 11.4 million followers. Okay!

All that to say that execs and producers are constantly on the search for gaps to fill and trends to follow. And if you're a writer or director, one path for you is to try to fill those orders.

This week, Elaine Low over at The Ankler published an insightful story on one audience that's being left behind in the TV landscape.

Can you fill this particular gap? Let's look closer.

- YouTube www.youtube.com

What the Research Says

The Ankler posits that young boys, once they age out of kids' shows like Bluey, inherit a media landscape dominated by video games, superhero franchises, and manosphere content creators. Low points to new audience research suggesting this isn't what young viewers are asking for.

The research she's citing is the 2025 Teens & Screens report from UCLA's Center for Scholars & Storytellers, a nationwide survey of 1,500 adolescents ages 10 to 24.

What it shows is a demographic hungry for a kind of story that Hollywood is not providing. Filmmakers and TV writers, if you're looking for an underserved audience, check out these results.

The report was authored by researchers Matt Puretz and Alisha Hines and CSS founder Yalda Uhls. Uhls is a developmental psychologist and former executive at MGM and Sony. Data was collected in August 2025.

The biggest findings include:

  • 59.7% of adolescents aged 14 to 24 said they want more content where the central relationships are friendships.
  • 60.9% want romantic relationships that are "more about the friendship between the couple than sex."
  • 54.9% want cross-gender characters who "prioritize their friendship instead of turning it into a romantic relationship." Among under-18s, that number climbs to 57.7%.
  • Friendship ranked third of 19 topics adolescents want to see. Romance ranked third-to-last.
  • 48.4% said there's too much sexual content in movies and TV.

Also, 57% of the surveyed adolescents said they watch traditional media more than older generations think, and 53% said they discuss TV and movies with their friends more often than they discuss social media content.

So what's another big takeaway? This isn't a demographic that's checked out of TV. They're just not being served.

'Reservation Dogs' Credit: Shane Brown/FX

What Young Men Are Asking For

CSS' follow-up, Gen Alpha and Gen Z: Evolving Masculinity, pulled additional questions from the same 2025 survey data.

The study found that young audiences (including men) want to see male characters who are emotionally available, vulnerable, and capable of connection rather than dominance.

Uhls said in UCLA's press release:

"Our findings reveal a profound cultural shift: Youth are craving a version of masculinity defined by emotional availability and joyful connection. By highlighting these narratives of partnership and care, storytellers can offer a vision of masculinity rooted in hope and love. For today’s young audiences, the most compelling hero isn’t the one standing alone, but the one who has the courage to be present."

Co-author Matt Puretz said that the preference holds across the age range.

"It might be easy for someone making a teen or young adult show to say: This really only applies to younger kids. But we see from ages 15 to 24, young people still prefer nurturing, emotionally available men, who serve as positive models of masculinity for them."

What Is the Industry Offering?

Not much, as The Ankler notes, is available to kids graduating from Bluey, effectively forcing them to skip to adult fare. Producers and exec Low spoke to mentioned that rewatches were big for family viewing since there hasn't been anything new in a while. Shows like Stranger Things, Malcolm in the Middle, and Modern Family are in the rotation. (We'd add Reservation Dogs and Ted Lasso to the safe watch list, but both are still years old at this point.)

It might be for this reason that many assume (or hear from their friends with kids) that their sons are just playing video games, scrolling social media, or on YouTube. There's a sense of instant gratification, even if the content isn't TV-caliber. It's what they want, and it's right in front of them at a click.

Pew Research figures cited by Blank Spaces' 2026 YouTube screen-time report show 93% of teen boys use YouTube (vs. 87% of teen girls), and 19% of teen boys use it "almost constantly" (nearly double the rate for girls).

On the gaming side, Pew data (via IconEra) show that video game participation among U.S. teenage boys is 97%, with 61% gaming daily. Compare that to 22% of teenage girls gaming daily.

Meanwhile, traditional TV is losing this audience, even as the 2025 Teens & Screens data shows they still want stories. They're just consuming those stories on platforms Hollywood doesn't produce for.

Add yet another wrinkle. Those platforms are pivoting fast. Netflix now views YouTube (not Disney+ or Paramount) as its main competitor, and AlixPartners' 2026 Media & Entertainment Industry Predictions Report argues the two platforms are converging. YouTube is moving toward Netflix-style long-form, while Netflix is putting everything on its platform, from games to podcasts and creator content.

In July 2026, Netflix started adding licensed publisher videos to its platform, a direct aim at the casual-viewing habits of YouTube fans.

Meta is doing the same thing from the opposite direction. TechCrunch reported in June 2026 that Meta is testing a "Series" feature on Instagram and Facebook, letting creators turn Reels into episodic content. Each Reel becomes an episode.

The feature mirrors TikTok's own Series product, which launched in 2023 and now supports videos up to 20 minutes.

Don't get us started on verticals or we'll be here all day.

The point is, if traditional TV doesn't build for this audience, YouTube and Meta will.

This is not specifically a mandate, because as Low covers, execs want safe bets, so they're mostly going for superheroes. And it's hard to write to an audience. But as you're brainstorming, you might consider—if you're writing for kids, are you going to be able to connect with them? Because they're telling us what they want.

blogs.title: Your Edit Isn’t Finished Until It Sounds Right
blogs.description:
Think about a scene you remember vividly: footsteps getting louder as someone approaches, the sudden drop in music before a reveal, or the crunch of leaves under someone’s shoes. These details might not be what you notice first, but take them away, and the scene immediately feels different.

For years, sound has often been treated as one of the final steps in the creative process. You get the picture right, lock the edit, and then figure out the music, dialogue, and sound effects.

But what if there was a simpler way for sound to be part of the creative process from the start?

With Firefly's popular audio tools including Generate Music, Generate Speech, and Generate Sound Effects, creators can experiment with sound earlier, using it to shape pacing, test an idea, or understand how a scene feels before everything is locked.

Using Sound to Shape a Story

That's the idea behind Adobe Firefly's new audio capabilities. With Generate Music, Generate Speech and Generate Sound Effects, creators can experiment with sound while an edit is still taking shape, using it to test creative directions, shape pacing and get a better sense of how a scene feels before everything is locked.

With Generate Music, creators can generate original, fully licensed tracks based on the mood and length of their video. Instead of waiting until the end of an edit to find the right music, an editor can try a few different directions early on and see how each one changes the tone of a scene. A podcaster might generate original intro, outro, and transition music, while a wedding or event videographer can explore a track that follows the emotional arc of a highlight reel.

Generate Speech offers a similar opportunity with voiceover. Creators can turn a script into natural-sounding narration, with options from Adobe's Firefly speech model and ElevenLabs. A producer can use a generated voiceover as a temporary track to test pacing, while a gaming creator can experiment with a distinct voice for a new character before committing to a final recording.

Generate Sound Effects can also become part of the editing process, creating custom sounds based on the action, timing, and energy of a scene. A travel vlogger can add the crunch of leaves to a camping sequence, while a motion designer can test a subtle whoosh or click to give a product animation more movement.

The point isn't simply to make sound faster. It's to make it easier to experiment with sound while you're still making creative decisions. A music cue can change the pace of a scene, a voiceover can reveal that a sequence needs more room to breathe, and a well-placed sound effect can change the rhythm of a transition. With Firefly, those decisions don't have to wait until the very end of the edit.

From First Idea to Final Sound

Audio is one part of Firefly's broader approach to creative AI: giving creators tools to explore an idea across different types of media in one place.

Instead of moving between different apps and services to find an image, video, music track or sound effect, creators can explore different creative directions within Firefly, using Adobe's own models alongside a growing selection of industry-leading models from Adobe, Google, Kling AI, Luma AI, OpenAI, Runway and others.

That flexibility matters because creative work rarely happens in a straight line. An idea changes as you see it, hear it and start to put the pieces together. And sometimes the best way to figure out what a story needs is to simply try it.

When sound can be part of that experimentation from the beginning, it becomes more than the final layer on an edit. It becomes another creative tool for figuring out what the story wants to be.

blogs.title: Iconic Film Character Intros: Mildred Hayes - The Moment You Know She Won’t Back Down
blogs.description:
Martin McDonagh’s 2017 masterpiece, Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri, boasts some of the finest character work of the entire decade. Frances McDormand’s Oscar-winning performance as Mildred Hayes, a grieving yet vengeful mother, is the film’s north star. Her opening scene also tells us everything we need to know about her.

Let’s dive right in.

Her Confidence is Unrelenting

The first time we see Mildred, she’s driving past the abandoned billboards near her house. She makes an internal decision almost immediately, then marches straight into the local advertising agency to instruct them to put up the billboards. She knows what they want to say, how much she’s paying for them, and what she needs her contract to say so that no one (the police) tries to buy her space out from under her.

You can see the moment everything changes for her in the opening scene while she’s staring at the billboards. Her face and body appear plagued by defeat and pain, her hair is long and nearly-matted, and the last thing you would assume about her is her personality for the rest of the film. The moment she springs into action, her hair gets put up, she wears more active clothing, and her general demeanor evolves into generally looking like she’s ready for intense battle.

Her Aggression Isn’t Unprovoked

‘Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri’Credit: Searchlight Pictures

Nearly every character in the film is at the very least weary, and at most, terrified of Mildred Hayes. These feelings are far from unfounded, as her reputation of being successful with her aggression certainly precedes her. With that said, she never comes at someone unprovoked.

While in the advertising agency, Red Welby (Caleb Landry Jones) makes the mistake of questioning whether or not Mildred understands the strangeness of her billboard request. Granted, all she does in this moment is snap back at him with a quip about his intelligence, or lack thereof, but it’s certainly a sign of what to expect from her in the future. Her priest insults her brigade, and she goes on a monologue about how he’s culpable for Catholic pedophilia; a high-schooler throws a drink on her car, so she kicks him where the sun doesn’t shine; the list goes on. But with all of that said…

She is Also Incredibly Gentle

The moment Red realizes what the billboards are supposed to say, he recognizes Mildred. Mildred acknowledges that he’s correct in a much more somber tone before helping a struggling beetle on its back flip properly upright. This quick 180 demonstrates not only a serious level of depth for the character, but the versatility of McDormand’s performance itself.

We see this deeply impactful sense of empathy multiple other times throughout the film. Most meaningfully, it manifests in her largely tumultuous relationship with William Willoughby (Woody Harrelson), the sheriff of the town she’s calling out with her billboards. He’s doomed to die from cancer at the start of the film, and during a particularly heated conversation between the two, he coughs up blood onto her face. Her demeanor immediately changes from aggressive and wanting to destroy him to fading into pure motherly protection. What’s most interesting about this is that a bit later in the film we’re clued into how this level of empathy may not have always been her kneejerk instinct.

Her Past Aggression Likely Cost Her Her Daughter

‘Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri’Credit: Searchlight Pictures

In the only flashback scene in the film, we see Mildred fighting with her daughter, Angela, about borrowing the family car to go to a function on the night she was murdered. Mildred’s sense of wit and aggression are still present, but her ability to remain as empathetic during a confrontation as we know her doesn’t seem to be there yet. The conversation ends with Angela storming out with her and Mildred “agreeing” that they “hope [she gets] raped on the way”. Devastatingly, that’s exactly what happened.

We never see Mildred address this conversation to herself, or anybody else throughout the film, but it’s easy to infer that the fragmented relationship she had with her daughter immediately prior to her death eats away at her soul more aggressively than even she can probably vocalize.

How Mildred’s Ending Affects Everyone Else’s

There are a lot of people going through a lot of dark stuff throughout the film. Officer Jason Dixon (Sam Rockwell) has a reputation around town for his past racist behavior and is struggling to grieve the death of Willoughby in the second half while forging his own redemption path.

There comes a moment in the final minutes of the film where he phones Mildred some bad news, and he appears to be holding his rifle to his head while he does so. Whether he meant to do anything to himself in this moment remains relatively unclear; however, what is clear is that he puts the gun down when Mildred not only takes the news better than he anticipated, but extends an olive branch for their reconciliation. It took Mildred an incredible amount of grace to be able to handle this conversation as well as she did. And doing so may have just saved Dixon’s life.

While the closing scene of the film leaves the explicit endings of both of these characters relatively open-ended, it’s abundantly clear that they’ve found some sort of a sense of peace at the end of their journey.

blogs.title: Rob Reiner's Coming-of-Age Masterpiece Turned 40 Years Old This Month
blogs.description:
Stand by Me, the adaptation of the Stephen King short story “The Body” that was directed by the late, great Rob Reiner, debuted in theaters on August 22, 1986. However, even though it turned 40 years old this month, it remains one of the most potent coming-of-age dramas in cinema history.

In honor of its anniversary, let’s break down what makes the movie so very special.

Stand by Me Came in the Middle of the Reiner Run

Right off the bat, one thing that makes Stand by Me special is the fact that it is part of one of the greatest uninterrupted runs of great movies by a single director. The “Reiner Run,” which lasted from the mid-1980s through the early 1990s, saw the director churn out seven towering classics in a row. What makes the run even more impressive is the fact that almost all of those movies occupy entirely different genres.

After kicking off this run with the iconic rock music mockumentary This is Spinal Tap in 1984 (which was his feature debut after establishing himself as an actor, most notably playing Michael "Meathead" Stivic on the smash hit Norman Lear sitcom All in the Family from 1971 through 1979), Rob Reiner helmed the 1985 John Cusack teen comedy The Sure Thing, which he of course followed with Stand by Me.

Next up was 1987’s The Princess Bride, a fantasy romance that contributed innumerable iconic quotes to the lexicon of cinema fans, followed by the seminal 1989 romantic comedy When Harry Met Sally (which remains such a go-to reference that it was quoted in this year’s Ryan Gosling sci-fi hit Project Hail Mary), then the 1990 Kathy Bates horror hit Misery (Reiner’s Stephen King adaptation) and the 1992 legal drama A Few Good Men.

Even among such celebrated contemporaries, Stand by Me stands out as a confident masterwork that taps directly into a universal sense of childhood nostalgia.

What Is It About Stand by Me?

Stand by Me has a deceptively low-key story for a movie that looms so large. In short, it follows the adventures of four friends who embark on a journey to see a dead body. However, it spins this quotidian childhood tale out into an intricately layered odyssey.

It obviously doesn’t hurt that this story is brought to life by an ensemble cast that was a shockingly deep bench of established and rising stars. The four major characters are played by Wil Wheaton (Star Trek: The Next Generation), River Phoenix (My Own Private Idaho), Corey Feldman (The Goonies), and Jerry O’Connell (Scream 2), but the movie also features Kiefer Sutherland (24) as bully Ace Merrill, Richard Dreyfuss (Jaws) as the adult version of Wheaton’s character Gordie, and John Cusack as Gordie’s older brother Denny.

‘Stand by Me’ (1986)Credit: Columbia Pictures

The story is given depth thanks to the performances and the cast’s chemistry with one another, but it is also imbued with meaning thanks to the many thematic threads that are carefully woven together in the screenplay by Raynold Gideon and Bruce A. Evans (who had previously collaborated on John Carpenter’s Starman).

These themes all revolve around the theme of coming of age and that precarious moment where one is still technically a child, but needs to develop the tools they need in order to handle adult problems (including death and growing apart). This is evoked exquisitely by the fact that the entire story is presented as the bittersweet recollections of the adult Gordie, who is writing a story about his friends.

In addition to the thrust of the story quite literally being about looking death in the face, throughout its runtime, the movie examines various forms of masculinity. This includes the vast dynamics between different pairs of the four main boys (most notably the vulnerable moment that Gordie and River Phoenix’s character Chris share) as well as the homosocial dynamics of Ace’s gang, who are shown carving tattoos into one another’s skin during a key moment in the movie.

Rob Reiner could have easily just stayed out of the way of the cast and the screenplay and called it a day, but the director was hardly content to do that ever, let alone when he was at the height of his powers. The work he does in Stand by Me is subtle, but enormously powerful, using every chance he gets to visually distinguish the four protagonists from one another, deepening every dialogue-driven interaction by constantly reinforcing their personas visually.

This is most notable in the sequences where the boys are all shown performing the same action, with the differences in their approach highlighting the ways that each of them approach the world. This happens constantly throughout the film, including the infamous sequence where they boys run away from a speeding train.

In the scene, O’Connell’s character Vern panics while Gordie helps him along, in spite of the fact that he is in the back of the group and therefore in the most danger. Meanwhile, Chris and Feldman’s Teddy Duchamp run for their lives without looking back, with Chris egging Teddy on. Only once they get to safety do they focus on their friends and shout words of encouragement. In one quick, two-minute sequence, the audience learns everything they need to know about the characters and where they stand at that point in the movie, all thanks to Reiner’s masterful staging.

The Legacy of Stand by Me Stands Strong

Stand by Me was a critical and commercial success in its own time, grossing $52.3 million and becoming the 13th highest grossing movie of the year at the domestic box office (above a number of other major titles, including Pretty in Pink, Cobra, Poltergeist II, Peggy Sue Got Married, The Fly, and Friday the 13th Part VI: Jason Lives), going on to be nominated for an Oscar for Best Adapted Screenplay (though it lost to A Room with a View).

It has maintained its momentum more or less consistently in the 40 years since it first burst onto the scene. Even Reiner himself kept the flame alive, naming his production company Castle Rock Entertainment after the fictional town in which the movie takes place.

This means that a title card bearing a reference to Stand by Me has appeared in front of dozens of major releases over the years, including When Harry Met Sally, Before Sunrise, Best in Show, Miss Congeniality, The Bucket List, and numerous other Stephen King movies like The Shawshank Redemption, Dolores Claiborne, and Needful Things.

Stand by Me has also gone on to directly inspire filmmakers throughout the ages, being homaged in everything from Boyz n the Hood (director John Singleton told Vice that it was “the last film I saw before I started college” and that it “affected me emotionally,” inspiring both the general shape of his debut feature as well as directly inspiring a scene where the main characters discover a body) to Netflix’s Stranger Things (according to The Express Tribune, the hit show’s creators, The Duffer Brothers, had the male actors audition with scenes from the Reiner classic) to Pixar’s Luca (per Looper).

So where do you think Stand by Me stands among the other classics from the Reiner Run, and will you be giving it a watch in honor of its anniversary? Sound off in the comments below!

blogs.title: Have You Seen This Killer Dinosaur Movie From the ‘90s?
blogs.description:
The End of Oak Street (2026) is the most recent “man vs. nature” blockbuster that swaps out modern-day animals and brings in dinosaurs for an extra dose of fun and fear that a bear or a shark can’t really compete with. It’s not the first time, nor will it be the last, that this what-if plot gets made into a movie.

Jurassic Park is easily the winner on how to do the concept well in giving audiences both the sense of wonder and the terror of humans trying to survive among prehistoric creatures. But genetically engineered dinosaurs weren’t just in that Spielberg film from 1993. A B-movie about killer dinos was released into theaters one month earlier.

Carnosaur went for the jugular, literally, with its batch of resurrected dinos. They were hungry for human flesh. Legs were bitten off, heads too. While Jurassic Park had Laura Dern as a lead, Carnosaur starred Dern’s mother, Diane Ladd, as a sinister mad scientist.

If you want a creature feature with a weird government conspiracy and a vicious kill count, Carnosaur is the one for you.

Two Different Dinosaur Movies

Jurassic Park is based on the 1990 novel by Michael Crichton, and it is considered a timeless classic that has given us memorable characters with quotable lines, cutting-edge CGI effects, and that nostalgic score by John Williams. It’s one of those movies where you react with shock if you find out someone you know has never seen it. It’s far more likely that someone has never seen the other dinosaur movie of ‘93.

Carnosaur is loosely based on the novel of the same name by John Brosnan, published in 1984, six years before Crichton’s work. It went on to get two sequels and two spin-offs, but it’s clear within the first ten minutes why this movie didn’t end up stomping into pop culture like Jurassic Park did.

Dinosaurs and Mad Science

Carnosaur begins with mysterious animal attacks near the town of Climax, Nevada. Genetically altered chickens give birth to baby dinosaurs, which rapidly grow and attack the locals. The police are baffled, and things get worse when the women in town get sick with a fever.

‘Carnosaur’ (1993)Credit: New Horizon Pictures

Caught in the middle are Doc (Raphael Sbarge), the overnight guard of an excavation site, and Thrush (Jennifer Runyon), a stubborn environmentalist. How the attacks and illness are connected leads to experiments in a laboratory run by Dr. Jane Tiptree (Ladd). It’s a conspiracy that will trigger doomsday.

The production of Carnosaur was hatched by executive producer Roger Corman, the king of low-budget B-movies, who helped the early careers of directors Martin Scorsese and James Cameron. Corman had also produced 1978’s Piranha as a ripoff of Jaws, so it shouldn’t be all that surprising that he made Carnosaur in anticipation of the success of Jurassic Park.

Prehistoric Mayhem

‘Carnosaur’ (1993)Credit: New Horizon Pictures

Carnosaur was released on May 21, 1993, a few weeks before Jurassic Park hit theaters on June 9. And they couldn’t be more different. That was intentional on the part of Carnosaur’s director and writer, Adam Simon, who talked about the use of graphic violence that he knew wouldn’t be in Spielberg’s movie.

“It seemed to me that dinosaur movies are usually so much about the sense of wonder of the dinosaurs that even if you’re afraid of them, they’re not that gory,” Simon said in an interview with Dread Central. His inspirations? The body horror of Alien and the movies by David Cronenberg.

The Creatures of Carnosaur

‘Movie Magic’ (1994)Credit: Discovery Channel

John Carl Buechler led the special effects team in creating the puppets and life-sized models of the Deinonychus and the Tyrannosaurus rex that have an appetite for humans. There are no actual Carnosaurs, as the title was taken from an outdated classification. And it didn’t have Jurassic Park’s budget, put around $63 million, or the two years of pre-production that were spent on designing the dinosaurs.

According to Simon, the budget for Carnosaur was under $1 million, and scenes from the script had to be cut due to this. In the documentary TV show, Movie Magic, the third episode of Season 1 featured Buechler and his team, where they were given only ten weeks to design and build the creatures for Carnosaur.

While the dinos can look good (and monstrous) in their close-ups, when they move, they look cheesy. The editing helps with the limitations in fast cuts during the grisly attack scenes. When Thrust and her group of environmentalists chain themselves to excavation equipment, they don’t expect to encounter a T.rex, who tears into the group, biting off limbs, leaving Thrust as the only survivor.

The most surprising part of Carnosaur is how dark it gets with the government conspiracy.

Diane Ladd’s Chilling Performance

‘Carnosaur’ (1993)Credit: New Horizon Pictures

Dr. Tiptree’s contempt for people has led her to orchestrate humanity’s extinction by resurrecting dinosaurs to reclaim the Earth. In every scene, Ladd is captivating as the mad scientist. Her acting even garnered a positive reaction from notable film critics, Roger Ebert and Gene Siskel, on their TV series, At the Movies.

During the segment for Carnosaur, Ebert panned it, but he was in agreement with Siskel, who praised what Ladd brought to the role. Siskel even mentioned Jurassic Park’s upcoming release at the time of the episode. He knew it was going to have “high-tech dinosaurs,” but he wondered if it would have “any humans as enjoyable as Diane Ladd’s character.”

Tiptree’s doomsday agenda is pure shlock. Her lab is more of a supervillain lair, with a laser cage holding in a T.rex. But Ladd pulls back from going over-the-top. She plays Tiptree with a soft-spoken voice and a calm head, as the end of the world is initiated by her prehistoric creations. Her fate is just as bonkers too, yet that can describe everything else in this movie.

The World of Carnosaur Is Bleak

‘Carnosaur’ (1993)Credit: New Horizon Pictures

If the people of the Nevada town aren’t shredded, the women soon become pregnant with the creatures (likely the inspiration that Simon took from Alien).

There is a shady government agency that wants to cover up what Dr. Tiptree is doing: in a bizarre scene, an official is sprawled on a table as he presents genetically altered blueberry pie to a senator for a taste test. There is a showdown between a sheriff and the Deinonychus, and a showdown between the T.rex and a skid loader. However, the grim and shocking ending won’t be spoiled here. You have to see it for yourself.

Sure, Jurassic Park is famous for the CGI effects, as well as countless other trivia facts. It also wanted the dinosaurs to behave like wild animals, not movie monsters. Carnosaur wasn’t as sentimental, fully leaning into the calamity of humans becoming food to prehistoric predators.

Maybe it’s time for a double feature?

blogs.title: The 'Matrix' Scene That Made Keanu Reeves a Legend
blogs.description:
The Matrix has been a cultural phenomenon ever since the first film was released in 1999. Keanu Reeves’ performance as the titular hero, Neo, is one that has often been parodied and referenced in popular culture. Reeves isn’t exactly known for his stellar acting chops, and yet, it’s impossible to imagine anyone else taking the role.

Let’s talk about why, as well as the specific moment that etched him into cinema history.

The Hero’s Journey Character Structure

It’s one of the oldest tricks in the screenwriting toolbox. Take someone ordinary who longs for something extraordinary, and place them on a really difficult journey that will eventually lead them down that path. Neo’s journey is far from complete by the end of the first film, but the amount of growth we see him go through and the strength that we see him develop by the end of the film is very easy to be inspired by.

His character starts out literally “trapped in the Matrix”. He works a boring office job that he hates, his managers are snippy with him, he makes shady dark-web style dealings for hackers on the side, and doesn’t have a ton of prospects that match his potential.

Once recruited by Morpheus, his extensive training and combat experience against the diabolical Agent Smith and his counterparts make for a thrilling journey, with everything coalescing into Neo coming into his own as the prophesied “One,” as his name is not-so-subtly an anagram of.

Playing to Keanu Reeves’ Strengths

‘The Matrix Reloaded’Credit: Warner Bros. Pictures

Keanu Reeves, as mentioned earlier, isn’t exactly known for his acting gravitas. Whenever directors place him in more dialogue-heavy, serious, deeply substantive roles, his performance begins to falter. He has a way of delivering dialogue that, while iconic, isn’t a style most performers find themselves replicating all that often. The roles outside of The Matrix that he played prior to it that people reference the most tend to be his roles in films like Speed or Point Break, although that film still has some phenomenal line readings.

The Matrix understands Keanu’s strengths as an actor better than any movie he’s ever done. His dialogue is quick, snappy, and often quotable: perfect for him. And the important stuff comes in his physical work. The kung-fu, action combat, and maybe most importantly…the wardrobe.

Pretty Much the Entire Third Act of the Movie

The last 45 minutes of the first Matrix film boasts some of the coolest American action filmmaking ever produced at the time, and at the center of it all is Keanu Reeves in the impossibly cool all-black outfit with his trenchcoat and glasses. It’s an instantly recognizable fit to this day, and, as trivial as it may sound, this outfit plays such a huge role in how cool this guy looks during the lobby shootout.

The lobby shootout, once again, is one of the most iconic action sequences put to screen. If you look at any action movie made in the immediate half-decade post-1999, odds are there is going to be some form of ripoff to either that scene, or the third act of the film in general. The slo-mo, the music, the gymnastics, Keanu’s sunglasses, it’s a perfect storm of pure cool. And in my opinion, it’s not even in the top five coolest things that happen in the last act of the movie.

Combing through all of the craziness for a personal favorite moment can prove to be laborious, but it’s clear that the most iconic moment that has most stood the test of time is Keanu’s bullet gymnastics. Being able to have a moment so ingrained into culture like that all to yourself is something that so many of even the greatest performers of all time only dream of having.

Keanu Reeves in the 21st Century

‘John Wick’Credit: Lionsgate

The Matrix sequels certainly helped to maintain the public’s image of Reeves as a stoic, punk-rock action hero far into the early 2000s and beyond. So much so that his next big role as killer assassin John Wick, who made his debut in 2014, sports a very similar fashion style and even fewer words out of his mouth. The franchise took what made Keanu the coolest guy around in The Matrix and made a billion-dollar franchise out of it, with spinoffs and TV shows galore into the 2020s.

We can talk day in and day out about that franchise as well, and how much Keanu makes it so special. But the important thing to remember is, we wouldn’t have any of it without the not-so-little punk sci-fi movie that could in 1999.

blogs.title: Film Quote of the Day: The 'Gladiator' Line That Reveals Why Cicero Remained Loyal to Maximus
blogs.description:
If you've been craving more Odysseus-style adventures after this summer, Gladiator is definitely a historical epic that can sate your cravings for action, epic drama, and old-school political intrigue.

The film was released in 2000. It stars Russell Crowe, Joaquin Phoenix, and Connie Nielsen, and was directed by Ridley Scott from a script by David Franzoni, John Logan, and William Nicholson. Franzoni was the original writer who received an Oscar nomination for this work, while Logan and Nicholson were brought on at various stages to do polishes.

The story is a fairly simple one. Maximus Decimus Meridius (Crowe) is a celebrated Roman general beloved by Caesar Marcus Aurelius (Richard Harris). So beloved, in fact, that the ruler decides to give Maximus the kingdom to lead as a democracy, overlooking his own troubled son Commodus (Phoenix). When Commodus learns of this, he murders his father and tries to have Maximus killed too. Maximus escapes, but learns his family has been murdered, and he is later captured as a slave.

"The hero builds up against the impossible machine," Franzoni told Creative Screenwriting. "You have two choices. You can be like Jack Nicholson in Five Easy Pieces where you go hitchhiking and prevail against the inevitable, or you can be like him in One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest where you go up against Nurse Ratched, you can't possibly win, and are destroyed."

One early scene, before the tragedy begins, lays out the film's theme, which is what we're looking at today.

Gladiator. Do what I have to do.#gladiator #maximus #cicero #honour #loyalty #dignity #duty youtube.com

The Scene

The film opens with an epic battle in which Maximus delivers Germania to Aurelius. Caesar arrives and makes camp with the armies. A dying Marcus Aurelius asks Maximus to become protector of Rome, and Maximus answers, "With all my heart, no," because what he wants is his farm, his wife, his son.

Commodus and his sister Lucilla (Nielsen) are also at the camp. Maximus passes Lucilla, and their conversation hints at a romantic past.

In his own tent, Maximus prays at his altar. "Ancestors, I ask for your guidance. Blessed Mother, come to me with the gods' desire for my future. Blessed Father, watch over my wife and son with a ready sword. Whisper to them I live only to hold them again."

His servant, Cicero (Tommy Flanagan), is with him. Maximus calls him over.

"You don't find it hard to do your duty?" he asks.

Cicero responds, "Sometimes I do what I want to do. The rest of the time I do what I have to."

Maximus sits with this.

"We may not be able to go home after all."

What the Line Reveals about Cicero

"Sometimes I do what I want to do. The rest of the time I do what I have to."

Cicero does not get a ton of screen time in this film, but he's vital, and he's always been one of my favorite characters. A moment later, when Commodus' men come for Maximus, Cicero is at the ready with his sword. His master waves him off with a subtle nod and allows himself to be taken.

Cicero is all about duty over desire, which is expressed by this line. He does what he wants to do sometimes. The rest of the time, he does what he must. And staying loyal to Maximus until death, regardless of his master's standing as general or slave, is what he feels he must do. There is familiarity and love here, but there's also obligation he chooses to follow.

Cicero is the humble version of the code the film puts forward: honor, duty, loyalty, and sacrifice.

'Gladiator' Credit: Dreamworks Distribution LLC

The Line Is Really About Maximus

In Franzoni's original script, Cicero does not exist, nor does this scene. It's a quiet beat to make Maximus' desire clear and to give him a moment to grapple with the decision in front of him.

Maximus asks whether Cicero finds duty hard because duty is tearing him apart. It's clear he's about to choose Rome over home, and the button on the scene betrays this.

Cicero, his plainspoken confidant, provides the stoic ideal Maximus is straining to reach. Maximus just doesn't yet know the decision has been made for him, and he's about to lose everything.

If you want to externalize your protagonist's internal drama or conflict, you might give them a sounding board. Their dialogue can articulate a theme openly without self-narration.

Here, the servant answers, but the hero is the one being characterized. The line does double duty on speaker and listener. The question runs on subtext, not small talk. The balanced "sometimes I do X/the rest of the time I do Y" is antithesis that gives it rhythm and weight.

Loyalty to the End

The line predicts Cicero's actions. Near the end of the film, Maximus has gathered enough underground support as a gladiator to plan a rebellion and escape. Cicero, by then, has found him and helped put his plan in action. He is Maximus' link to his army at Ostia, and he waits with the horses to help take him away, and finally he gives his life when the plot unravels.

Cicero did not have to do any of that. He could have recognized his old master fighting in the arenas, and done nothing, and lived another life. But he goes to Maximus anyway. He's a hero of another kind.

Maximus is captured and fights for his life in a final battle, where he kills Commodus but gives his own life in the process. Lucilla is left to rebuild Rome in the way her father wanted all along.

Franzoni told Creative Screenwriting that he had to fight to give the characters their darker endings, with most of the "good guys" perishing in the end.

"Gladiator had to be Maximus' journey, not the studio executives' journey."

He added that writers should watch classic cinema and focus on telling stories about characters with lived lives.

"Then you understand why living a life gives you something to talk about rather than just mocking other stories. Our job as artists is to add to the wealth of humanity."

blogs.title: How Howard Hawks Pitted John Wayne Against Montgomery Clift to Redefine the Western
blogs.description:
I got this amazing Blu-ray and 4K disc player for my birthday, and I have been renting or buying 4K discs, utterly blowing my mind. One of the discs I snagged this week was the Criterion of Howard Hawks’ Red River (1948).

There is so much to say about this restoration, but today I wanted to focus on how Hawks took a cattle drive and used it as the literal driving force behind a psychological epic that redefined the American Western.

Before Red River, Howard Hawks was already a master of genre storytelling. The guy was sort of a Swiss Army knife of early Hollywood. If you needed a genre movie made, he was the number you dialed.

He had conquered the screwball comedy with Bringing Up Baby, the gangster movie with Scarface, and even film noir with The Big Sleep.

But Hawks had never made a Western, and eventually, the bill came due.

The thing I love about Hawks is that he was always himself behind the camera. So if he was going to do a genre, he wanted to do it his way. Red River is sort of the perfect auteur entry into the Western genre because it has all the Hawks' signature elements while also embracing the tropes that would define the genre going forward.

Let's dive in.

- YouTubewww.youtube.com

A Clash of Generations and Acting Styles

As I said at the start, Hawks was always himself behind the camera. Hawks was obsessed with professionalism and craft.

His films have incredible cinematography, and he was daring with how he moved the camera.

He also loved stories about ensembles and defined his characters by whether they could do their job well.

The movie is about a cattle drive that pulls apart the masculinity of its central characters the further they go, laying them bare before each other in ways they never could have imagined before setting out on the journey.

Our two characters going back and forth are Thomas Dunson (John Wayne) and his adopted son, Matt Garth (Montgomery Clift). Dunson and Matt’s feud isn't just emotional because of who they are; it's a disagreement over the right way to execute the drive, to do the job.

This is that Hawksian element that showcases the auteur's hand.

These two behemoths of the silver screen are clearly trying to one-up each other's acting in the movie, and that gives every scene a little extra mustard and tension.

What's even crazier is that it's one of their first films.

I think you could say John Wayne delivered a career-defining performance as Dunson. He takes the tyrannical cattle baron to new levels as he grows increasingly unhinged.

Wayne had been a star in Hollywood for over a decade and was used to getting his way on set. He was perfect in this role because he could push the other actors around, and that came across as sort of the meta-narrative of this movie.

And who can blame him? The bad luck on the trip is setting him and his business back as his farmhands desert him, his cows fall ill, and the drive to Missouri proves treacherous.

As I mentioned earlier, this is Montgomery Clift's film debut, and he's already going toe-to-toe with the biggest name in Westerns ever.

On set, Clift was a different actor than Wayne. He was quieter, internal, and intense.

This back-and-forth mirrored what Hollywood was facing post-war, as more actors were changing to this new style. Not to be outdone, Wayne uses his bravado to deepen his character and put Clift on edge.

Hawks kind of treats this movie like a war film about a military march, but using cows. We don't have the taming of the West, which came up in a lot of Westerns of the day, but the unraveling of the people, who are becoming less tame themselves.

The film captures the dust, physical exhaustion, and paranoia of months on the trail, climaxing in a famous, thunderous stampede triggered by a dropped sugar bowl.

Summing It All Up

I think Red River elevated the Western, not in a pretentious way, but it kind of showed filmmakers that you could use the genre to explore other realms of possibility. You could have it be a psychological thriller or a more personal story about people.

This ended up in the later decades, using the Old West as a setting and giving us some amazing other movies. And it opened Hawks' signature style of putting his own imprint on different genres as inspiration for filmmakers who followed, too.

Let me know what you think in the comments.
