blogs.title: 'Grand Theft Auto VI': Technical Revolution, Cinematic Narrative, and the Digital Culture War
blogs.description:
Everyone has one video game that defined their childhood and another that defined their adulthood. But for many people, that game has been Grand Theft Auto VI, which feels like we've been waiting decades for it.

Well, it's only been 13 years, so jokes on you!

Rockstar Games will debut the 26-minute trailer for the new GTA today on Netflix and will drop the game on November 19, 2026.

It's going to usher in a new era for gamers and, honestly, for graphics and storytelling too. Everyone is on the edge of their seats, waiting for the game promised to redefine real-time rendering capabilities, spatial storytelling, and virtual worldbuilding.

Yeah, that's a lot of expectations!

So we have a ton to cover today, from the trailer drop to the captured PlayStation 5 footage revealing massive technological leaps in lighting and crowd rendering to complex double-protagonist narrative structures, and from controversial marketing partnerships announced via Netflix Tudum to industry-wide battles over digital ownership, physical discs, and piracy; GTA 6 is pushing the envelope on every front.

Let's dive in.

The Technical Frontier

I am not an expert in video game tech, but everything I have read about GTA 6 makes me think we're about to take a leap forward in gaming graphics.

The technical ambition behind GTA 6 demonstrates how Rockstar’s proprietary RAGE engine has evolved to compete directly with movies and TV shows.

They wanted this to feel like you're playing and watching a movie, and from the footage we've seen so far, they've mostly succeeded via these key areas.

Dynamic Lighting and Global Illumination

This is what makes the footage we've seen look so realistic. GTA 6 implements hardware-accelerated ray tracing for both real-time global illumination and multi-surface reflections.

That means that your images change as you walk through different environments. They're sort of to feel more like the real world, to have slivers of light and shadows, and to mimic reflections.

We'll have neon and sun bouncing off things in the day and at night, as well as water volume refraction along ocean shorelines.

This is a step toward being totally immersive.

Dense Crowd Simulation & Contextual NPC AI

Every time I think about cognizant NPCs, I think about Dungeon Crawler Carl. But the term Non-Player-Character is straight from gaming.

And in GTA6, we're going to get the most advanced NPCs ever.

According to Dazed Digital's exclusive world analysis, GTA 6 features an unprecedented density of non-playable characters (NPCs) operating on contextual AI routines. That means they're kind of smart and will have their own unique routines and goals adjacent to your own in the game.

They'll react to weather shifts and whatever you're doing, as well.

'Grand Theft Auto VI'Credit: Rockstar

Narrative Architecture

At its core, GTA 6 continues Rockstar’s legacy of sharp satire. We're basically playing a game that is set to take down society, and to malpoon the world we live in.

I'm excited to listen to the radio in this version, not only to hear the new music tracks but also to hear the hilarious call-in shows and podcasts that will surely skewer modern culture.

Our Main Characters: Lucia and Jason

The game's narrative follows a Bonnie-and-Clyde-type story featuring two people named Lucia and Jason.

Netflix Tudum previewed the game's story, revealing that it centers on Jason and Lucia after an easy score goes wrong. They are forced to rely on each other to survive a criminal conspiracy spanning the state of Leonida, a place you travel through as you play these characters and perform missions.

This dual-character framing allows Rockstar to leverage themes of trust, economic desperation, and criminal ambition in a world obsessed with online clout.

Gameplay breakdowns featured in Mashable show seamless transitions between non-interactive cutscenes and real-time control. This eliminates traditional loading cuts and maintains visual continuity between these story scenes and playing scenes.

To me, that makes the game way more immersive and gets the player to engage right away.

The Marketing & Distribution Controversy

We'd be remiss if we didn't cover the online chatter around the game and the way it has been rolled out. As I said in the opening, it's been like 13 years since the game was promised.

So people are already wondering if it will actually drop in November. And they're also mad that the marketing has been around digital copies instead of discs, and so Netflix forward.

Now feels like a good time to mention you can watch a 26-minute trailer for the game on Netflix below if you follow the link.

The Backlash

Many gamers are annoyed that the trailer for the game is debuting on Netflix, which requires a subscription to watch it. For them, itfeelsl ike Rockstar is signing a deal to make money and to charge them more via Netflix or their enthusiasm for the game.

As reported by OtakuKart, online communities quickly mocked the "Netflix GTA 6 reminder" campaigns. Fans are jokingly saying they had already seen an extended look years ago due to massive development leaks, and we've seen even more leaks of the footage that was coming to Netflix as people try to get it out there for free.

The biggest fight is over the digital copies of the game, which many people think is outrageous.

The game will cost $100 for the special edition, and many gamers are worried this will be the new normal price tag. Secondary to that are the rumors and moves toward an all-digital future that eliminates physical game discs.

Coupled with that are the worries that when you debut a game digitally like this one, there will be microtransactions inside it where they want more money to play it to the fullest extent, instead of one price baked in.

Again, we have no gameplay details on this yet, but when you take a while to release a game, people talk, and that talk leads to worry.

People are very worried about preservation and consumer rights concerns.

If you buy something that doesn't come with a physical copy, do you actually even own it?

People online have argued for piracy, since owning it only digitally isn't technically ownership, so then illegally downloading it wouldn't actually be pirating.

These are the debates raging online.

The Defining Media Event of 2026

Look, I do think this game is going to live up to the hype, because I think we're seeing people talk so much about it that it is obviously affecting their lives.

As Grand Theft Auto VI approaches its November 19, 2026 launch, we're seeing more anticipation, and I want to know what the Netflix numbers for the debut will be when you can watch that trailer.

Compound that with all the invisible leaks online, and you have this palpable sense of people ready for the big reveal.

Maybe we'll look back at this game as the first step in a fully immersive world where you can play as anyone and do anything.

For storytellers and filmmakers watching from the sidelines, GTA 6 is a lesson in how technology, art, and commerce collide on the grandest possible stage.

And how you need to keep your fans happy at every level and deliver when you promise.

Let me know what you think in the comments.

blogs.title: A Massive List of Fall 2026 Grants, Labs & Fellowships
blogs.description:
About the Author: Lee Moss is a director, screenwriter and story consultant born in NYC and based in Dublin. For years, they have benefited from No Film School’s vetted grant/fellowship lists and are happy to pay it forward in this community.

If you’re ready to put down that Aperol Spritz and pick up your camera, we've got you. Our fall list includes deadlines for TV writing opportunities as well as labs, fellowships, and financial support for docs and narratives in all stages of production.

Opportunities are organized by regular deadline unless otherwise indicated – from September through early December – and by category: documentaries, narratives, and screenwriting. An asterisk(*) indicates an opportunity available in multiple categories.

As always, use your best judgment when deciding to apply.

Documentary

‘You Can’t Stop Spirit’Directed by Vashni Balleste; distributed by Reel South

Female Film Club*

The Female Film Club, a London-based organization created to foster community during the pandemic shutdown, is offering €10,000 in funding for female and non-binary-directed shorts from anywhere in the world. Narrative and documentary films at all stages of production and post are welcome. In addition to the cash grant, awardees will receive post-production services and support from Disauthority and Mo-Sys.

The project budget is allowed to be higher than the grant, but to ensure the film gets made, the filmmaker needs to have all additional funding in place by Sept 5th. The final winner will be announced at BFI in October 2026.

Application fee is £50.

Deadline: September 5

Screen Australia’s Documentary Production Program

If you're an Australian-based filmmaker, you’re probably already aware of Screen Australia. Their documentary production program awards grants of up to 80% of the total project budget, capped at $300,000 (AUD), for projects with a budget of $500,000 or less; or up to 65% for production budgets of more than $500,000.

A full list of Screen Australia’s funding opportunities can be found here. There are no fees to apply.

From Screen Australia:

“Screen Australia is committed to building equity into its programs and its engagement with the community. Gender equity, anti-racism, authentic story-telling, from and about under-represented groups, and inclusivity are priorities for Screen Australia. We expect that the lived experience portrayed through the narrative and characters are reflected within the key creative team. It is vital the creative team has the cultural authorship to tell the story so that the telling of the story is authentic. This will be taken into account when assessing applications.”

Deadline: September 24

First Flights Short Film Fund*

This fund, sponsored by Kodak, is offering grants of up to £7,000 in production funding to scripted and documentary short filmmakers worldwide. Awards will be given to projects which intend to be in production no more than six months after the deadline closes.

Filmmakers can also apply to shoot their project on 16mm film. Two winners of this category will each receive 5 x 400ft rolls of Kodak 16mm film stock, along with covered processing costs. Submission fee is £30.

Regular Deadline: September 30

National Film Board of Canada Filmmaker Assistance Program

Despite its unfortunate acronym, the Filmmaker Assistance Program (FAP) can be a lifesaver for Canadian citizens looking to get their short and feature-length documentaries over the finish line.

This program offers selected Canadian filmmakers the opportunity to travel to Montreal to complete a portion of their post-production in-house at Balmoral Studios. Services provided include post-production services and access to post-production equipment such as picture and sound editing suites, online editing services, title and credits design, sound effects, voice recording, mixing, access to the NFB archives, master copies, and authoring of a complete digital cinema package (DCP).

Filmmakers living within 150 km of Montreal must cover 10% of the total cost of requested post-production services. For filmmakers who live more than 150 km from Montreal but wish to travel to Montreal to access the services, the NFB waives the 10%.

Supported projects include ‘The Muse’, ‘In the Closet’ and ‘Saturday’. There is no fee to apply.

Deadline: October 10

Impact Partners Development/Production Funds

Impact Partners, a documentary equity investor since 2007, invests in the development of 8-12 documentary projects per year, reviewing projects on a rolling basis. They can provide $100,000-$300,000 per project for films with a director and producer attached that address urgent societal issues.

Applications begin with a Letter of Inquiry, and applicants should receive a response in 2-4 weeks. Supported films include ‘How to Survive a Plague’, ‘Mistress Dispeller’ and ‘Sugar Cane’. There are no listed submission fees.

From Impact Partners:

“We are looking for projects that tell strong, cinematic stories, explore the urgent issues and questions of our time, and have a clear point of view and artistic vision. Filmmakers can apply to the [development] fund for a variety of reasons as they get their projects off the ground, including development shoots, cutting a trailer or reel, conducting archival research, casting characters, etc.”

Deadline: Rolling

‘The Muse’Directed by Wanda Nolan, supported by the National Film Board of Canada Filmmaker Assistance Program

Yale Law School DocProject

Launched in 2018, The DocProject is a program of the Media Freedom and Information Access Clinic at Yale Law School. Under the guidance of experienced media lawyers, Yale law students provide filmmakers with pro bono legal research and advice from the earliest stages of their projects through rough-cuts.

Supported films include ‘Pay or Die’, ‘Hummingbirds’ and ‘How to Sue the Klan’. There is no fee to apply.

From DocProject:

“The project’s mission is twofold: to assist documentary filmmakers who would not otherwise have access to legal resources, and to train the next generation of media lawyers…The Clinic also assists in advancing filmmakers’ efforts to obtain access, in addition to advising on libel, privacy and other content concerns.”

Deadline: Rolling

Film Independent Non-Fiction Work In Progress Series

Finished your feature doc and looking for a test audience? Film Independent’s L.A. based screening series offers a place for filmmakers to share their projects and receive constructive feedback. Audiences are invited to watch films as they enter the final stages of editing, offering feedback via in-depth surveys and a moderated discussion, helping to ready their projects for festivals and distribution.

The program is open to filmmakers located anywhere, but the director and/or key members of the creative team must be able to attend the screening in person. Filmmakers must provide a full edit at the time of submission. There is a $25 application fee.

NOTE: Film Independent membership is not required when applying to Artist Development programs. However, all participants accepted into programs are required to join Film Independent at the standard annual General Membership rate of $105, in addition to the initial application fee.

Deadlines: Rolling and announced throughout the year. Calls go out approximately two months before a scheduled screening. Follow Film Independent to stay across.

Good Docs Educational Distribution Opportunity

Founded by documentary filmmaker Sarah Feinbloom in 2013, GOOD DOCS is an educational documentary distributor representing a wide collection of films that “do GOOD in the world.”

They work with established documentarians as well as emerging ones, promoting filmmakers for speaking engagements as well as screenings. Filmmakers can submit for distribution consideration directly on their website.

Films distributed by GOOD DOCS include ‘The Nest’, ‘Arrest the Midwife’ and ‘Between the Mountain and the Sky’. There is no fee to submit.

From GOOD DOCS:

“Our award-winning collection engages and inspires students by featuring rarely heard stories about individuals and communities working towards a more equitable world. We champion creative expression and complex films that provoke critical thinking.”

Deadline: Rolling

Reel South Multi-Platform Distribution

Reel South is a PBS documentary series and a platform for non-fiction filmmakers in the American South working within the region’s tradition of storytelling. Filmmakers based in the South are given priority, but all stories set in the South will be eligible.

Narrated and non-narrated films are considered along with first-person or point-of-view projects, observational films, and news documentaries. Both shorts and features will be considered for distribution.

Selected films will receive a license fee, series packaging, captioning, mastering, inclusion on the series website, promotion, and errors and omissions insurance coverage.

Distributed films include ‘Winn’, ‘Roleplay’ and ‘I’m The Girl – The Story of a Photograph’. There is no fee to apply.

From RS:

“REEL SOUTH reveals the South's proud yet complicated heritage, as told by a diversity of voices and perspectives, through the commission, curation, and distribution of feature-length and short documentaries.”

Deadline: Rolling

The Scottish Documentary Institute Consultancies

These free consultancy appointments are offered to documentary filmmakers based in Scotland, sponsored by the Scottish Documentary Institute. Topics include festival strategy, forum/market applications, funding strategy for shorts and features, pitching and story development advice.

Films that have benefitted from SDI consultancy include ‘The Islands and the Whales’, ‘16 Years Til Summer’ and ‘Traveling Light’

Deadline: Rolling

Narrative

‘Monochromatic’Directed by Karen Bryson supported by the the First Flights Short Film Fund

Female Film Club*

The Female Film Club, a London-based organization created to foster community during the pandemic shutdown, is offering €10,000 in funding for female and non-binary-directed shorts from anywhere in the world. Narrative and documentary films at all stages of production and post are welcome. In addition to the cash grant, awardees will receive post-production services and support from Disauthority and Mo-Sys.

The project budget is allowed to be higher than the grant, but to ensure the film gets made, the filmmaker needs to have all additional funding in place by Sept 5th. The final winner will be announced at BFI in October 2026.

Application fee is £50.

Deadline: September 5

Seriesfest/Shondaland Women’s Directing Mentorship

Founded in 2019, this program is designed to provide a career launchpad to U.S. and U.K.-based female directors with unique voices.

The 2027 winner will receive the opportunity to shadow a director on an episode of a Shondaland original series and will receive an all-access badge to SeriesFest Season 13.

Applicants must have 3 years of professional experience (in any professional role, not just director). Applicants who have previously directed a network series are ineligible.

Past awardees include Tamika Miller, Rachel Myers and Gia-Rayne Harris.

Application fee is $50.

Deadline: September 15

First Flights Short Film Fund*

This fund, sponsored by Kodak, is offering grants of up to £7,000 in production funding to scripted and documentary short filmmakers worldwide. Awards will be given to projects which intend to be in production no more than six months after the deadline closes.

Filmmakers can also apply to shoot their project on 16mm film. Two winners of this category will each receive 5 x 400ft rolls of Kodak 16mm film stock, along with covered processing costs. Submission fee is £30.

Regular Deadline: September 30

Shore Scripts Short Film Fund

Shore Scripts is offering a $15,000 production grant for a winning short film script, plus $4,000 in finishing funds to a separate winner.

Past awarded projects include ‘The Town’, ‘Salam’ and ‘Thirsty Girl’. Regular deadline application fee is $49.

From Shore:

“We started our Short Film Fund in 2016 to create another avenue to get screenwriters' work out there into the industry. Having your screenplay produced, and gaining that credit, is instrumental in the building of your career…The films we have produced have gone on to play at hundreds of film festivals including Sundance, Tribeca, Cannes, BFI London, Austin, Palm Springs, and Encounters and have won BAFTA and other major awards.”

Late Deadline: September 30

Pandora Short Film Grant

Sponsored by Panavision and Kodak, the Pandora Short Film Grant offers $12,000 to a U.S. Filmmaker towards the production of a short narrative film.

The grant winner and three finalists, who will also receive in-kind equipment support from Kodak and Panavision, are chosen blindly based on their script and pitch materials.

These final four will also receive one-on-one mentorship from established industry professionals who have made career-launching shorts.

2026 mentors will be writer/directors Alma Har’el, Lila Neugebauer, Lauren Wolkstein, Sarah Elizabeth Mintz and Chris Merola. The late deadline application fee is $40.

Late Deadline: October 1

Lynn Shelton “Of A Certain Age” Grant

A project-based award for women and non-binary directors, aged 39 or older, who are working on their first narrative feature. This unrestricted, $25,000 award seeks to recognize filmmakers for their distinct visions, storytelling and singularity.

Past grantees include Jing Zou, Erica Tremblay and Jessica Sanders. There is generally a $30 application fee.

From Of A Certain Age:

“The Lynn Shelton “Of A Certain Age” Grant was created…to honor the legacy of beloved filmmaker Lynn Shelton…Shelton often spoke of feeling inspired after seeing filmmaker Claire Denis speak at Northwest Film Forum and learning that Denis did not make her first feature until age 40. Shelton went on to make her own first feature film (We Go Way Back) at the age of 39. In the years since, she built a prolific canon of feature and television work and made an indelible mark on the landscape of American cinema.”

Deadline: October 3 (application opens September 5)

‘A Girl Unknown’Directed by Jing Zou, Lynn Shelton “Of A Certain Age” awardee

The Wave Grant

Established in 2023 by the Wavelength Studio, The WAVE (Women at the Very Edge) Grant is devoted to supporting emerging filmmakers from diverse backgrounds and perspectives to tell their own “great f**king story.”

Five U.S.-based recipients will receive a $5,000 seed grant for the production of their first short film, as well as mentorship and in-kind partnered services from Seed&Spark, Fujifilm, WeTransfer, and Nice Shoes.

Short narrative films of approximately 10 minutes will be considered. Production cannot be scheduled to begin before April 2026.

Applicants may have experience in the film industry but cannot have previously directed a scripted short or feature (student films are okay). There is no fee to apply.

Deadline: November 16 (applications open October 15th)

Black Artist Grant (UK)

Offered by the art platform Creative Debuts, this program offers no-strings-attached microgrants of £500 to support Black artists residing in the United Kingdom. Applications are no-fee, rolling, and a new recipient is chosen monthly.

From Creative Debuts:

“This grant has been set up because Black artists are systematically under-supported by the art world; by institutions, curators, the artist-led scene, major and minor funding bodies, the market, art schools, and by audiences too.

Creative Debuts recognises that a full institutional overhaul and dismantling of racist structures is required to transform the industry permanently, but they hope in a small way that this grant will help enable recipients to continue their artistic practice when the odds are so stacked against them.”

Deadline: Rolling

National Film Board of Canada Filmmaker Assistance Program*

Despite its unfortunate acronym, the Filmmaker Assistance Program (FAP) can be a lifesaver for Canadian citizens looking to get their animated projects over the finish line.

This program offers selected Canadian filmmakers the opportunity to travel to Montreal to complete a portion of their post-production in-house at Balmoral Studios. Services provided include post-production services and access to post-production equipment such as picture and sound editing suites, online editing services, title and credits design, sound effects, voice recording, mixing, access to the NFB archives, master copies, and authoring of a complete digital cinema package (DCP).

Filmmakers living within 150 km of Montreal must cover 10% of the total cost of requested post-production services. For filmmakers who live more than 150 km from Montreal but wish to travel to Montreal to access the services, the NFB waives the 10%.

Supported projects include ‘Bread Will Walk’, ‘After Us’ and ‘Corpus and the Wandering’. There is no fee to apply.

Deadline: October 10

Panavision's New Filmmaker Program

If you are a U.S. or Canada-based student or low-budget indie filmmaker, Panavision may supply you with a free camera package.

Panavision has four 16mm and two 35mm cameras which have been set aside from the rental pool and are permanently attached to the program. Digital cameras may also be considered, based upon availability.

Supported projects include ‘Palm Trees and Power Lines’, ‘Zana’ and ‘Dixieland’. There is no fee to apply.

Deadline: Rolling

Screenwriting

‘Union County’Written and directed by Adam Meeks, developed at the Film Independent Screenwriting Lab

Film Independent Screenwriting Lab

The Screenwriting Lab is a two-week workshop held in Los Angeles, designed to provide individualized story and career development for emerging screenwriters with a fiction feature screenplay.

Each Screenwriting Fellow is paired with a creative advisor, with whom they’ll work one-on-one and in group sessions. A variety of guest speakers are invited to screen and discuss their own films and offer career insights, and a final pitch event offers further opportunity for individualized feedback and interaction with industry executives.

Past Screenwriting Lab projects include Adam Meek’s ‘Union County ’, Robbie Pickering’s ‘Natural Selection ’, and Jing Ai Ng’s ‘Forge’. Past advisors include lab alum Chloè Zhao, Derek Cianfrance, and Andrew Ahn.

There is a $65 application fee.

Extended Deadline: September 14

MacDowell Spring/Summer Residency

MacDowell’s prestigious residency program has supported hundreds of artists since its founding in 1907. Artists are provided with a private studio, chef-prepared meals, and living accommodations on their 450-acre property in Peterborough, New Hampshire. Residencies last from 4-6 weeks.

Past screenwriting residents include Dee Rees, David Zellner, and Isabel Sandoval.

From MacDowell:

“About 300 artists in seven disciplines are awarded Fellowships each year, and the sole criterion for acceptance is artistic excellence. There are no residency fees, and need-based stipends and travel reimbursement grants are available to open the residency to the broadest possible community of artists.”

Deadline: September 10

Writer’s Access Support Staff Training Program

The Writers Guild Foundation, in partnership with TV writers and producers Tanya Saracho (Vida), Mike Royce (One Day at a Time), and Liz Hsiao Lan Alper (Day of the Dead), created this 14-week course to provide writers who are BIPOC, LGBTQ+, disabled, and over the age of 50, with the tools and education to become a writers’ assistant and script coordinator, resulting in meaningful employment opportunities.

Graduates of the program are added to an ongoing list of trained writers’ assistants and script coordinators that is made available to studios, networks, and showrunners, in order to increase the pool of eligible hires.

The program will take place between January and May of next year. Applicants must be available for classes, hosted online via Zoom, on Thursday evenings from 7-10 pm PT. Optional in-person meetups and networking events are held exclusively in Los Angeles. There is no fee to apply.

Deadline: September 13

The Barn Residency

Founded by Edward Albee, this residency in Montauk, Long Island, has been operating for almost 60 years. It exists to serve writers and visual artists from all walks of life by providing time and space in which to work without disturbance.

Open year-round, the one-month residency is designed to offer space to four creative persons at a time. Writers and Visual Artists each receive a generously sized private ensuite bedroom and a private studio. There are usually two visual artists and two writers staying together during a cycle. Stipends are also provided in the amount of $2500 per Fellow, which will be disbursed upon completion of the one-month residency period.

Screenwriters will be asked to submit a full manuscript no longer than 130 pages. There are no fees to apply.

Deadline: September 14

‘Lingua Franca’Written and directed by MacDowell alum Isabel Sandoval

New York Mills Cultural Center Retreat

Located in the historic Finnish-founded town of New York Mills, Minnesota, this residency welcomes one artist at a time for stays of two to six weeks in 2027, providing free housing and studio access in a quiet rural setting.

Artists stay in a cozy one-bedroom bungalow within walking distance of the Cultural Center and downtown New York Mills, equipped with workspaces, essentials, and wireless internet. Artists provide their own transportation and meals.

As part of their residency, the Artist in Residence will create and lead a community outreach program designed to engage local residents in the arts. This program could take the form of a workshop, reading, performance, or other interactive event held at the Cultural Center, offering participants a hands-on opportunity to explore the artist’s creative process and medium.

Participants are selected based on artistic merit, dedication to their craft, commitment to creative growth, and interest in developing community through the arts.

There are no fees to apply.

Deadline: October 1

Camargo Fellowship

Created in 1971 by the American artist and philanthropist Jerome Hill, this international fellowship offers 10-week residencies to established or mid-career artists and scholars from diverse backgrounds, engaged in projects with strong research-based components.

Located in Cassis, France, on the edge of the Mediterranean Sea, the Foundation not only provides time and space for the residents, but also initiates exchanges within the group and develops a collective spirit – one of the program’s distinctive features. The interactions developed among the program’s fellows are a vital element of this program.

Seven artists fellowships are awarded per year. Upcoming windows are for September-November 17, 2027, and February-May 2028. A 3500 EUR stipend is provided for the duration of the residency, as is funding for basic transportation to and from Cassis per Fellow.

Applicants should have maintained a professional practice for at least 5 years and should be able to demonstrate a track record of publications, exhibitions, credits, awards, and/or other grants. There is no fee to apply.

Deadline: October 1

New Harmony Residency

Taking place over 10 days in May 2027, this residency is held in the pastoral landscape of New Harmony, Indiana. 18 writers working in theatre, film, and television will receive artistic support, including dramaturgical meetings, collaborators willing to read pages, and time and space to work and dream.

Residents will stay in a private room with a full bathroom at the New Harmony Inn Resort and Conference Center. Roundtrip air and ground transportation to/from southern Indiana, as well as meals throughout the residency, are supplied. For parent artists, childcare support is available for dependents of any age. There is no fee to apply.

From New Harmony:

“For four decades, The New Harmony Project has acted on the belief that writers need more than deadlines and deliverables: they need time, space, community, and care. In a small town founded on the pursuit of a better world, writers are invited to step away from the pressures of everyday life, renew their creative practice, and devote themselves fully to the stories only they can tell.”

Deadline: October 1 (Applications open in early September)

The Ouray Film Sabbatical

Located in the mountain town of Ouray, Colorado, known as the “Switzerland of America,” this four-day gathering is a fully funded residential experience that provides creative support, rest, and community for ten filmmakers, writers, and programmers.

The sabbatical is hosted by Ouray International Film Festival founders and filmmakers Jared LaCroix, Jake Abell, and Ben Wiessner. 2027 on-site facilitators will include filmmaker Alexandria Bombach, Bill Ross IV, and Robie Flores.

Applicants will be asked about their creative journey and what they hope to get out of this sabbatical. They will also be asked for a work sample. There is a $45 application fee.

“A wonderful, valuable program for pretty much anyone in the independent film ecosystem. It's like a meeting of the minds between directors, producers, documentarians, writers, festival programmers, etc - but a meeting of the minds where you also go to hot springs, make crafts, and enjoy a beautiful little mountain town.”

-Sam Osborn, 2026 Ouray Fellow

Deadline: October 5

Blacklist/Cassian Elwes Independent Screenwriting Fellowship

Need a crazy story? This program awards one screenwriter with an all-expenses-paid trip to the 2027 Sundance Film Festival accompanied by producer Cassian Elwes. It is open to unrepresented feature writers with an independent sensibility who have made less than $5,000 in aggregate in their film or television writing careers.

While there are no additional fees to apply, applicants are required to upload a project onto the Blacklist website in order to be considered at a cost of $30

From Blacklist:

“The Blacklist will choose ten screenplays imbued with an independent spirit by unrepresented screenwriters, which will be sent on to Mr. Elwes for his consideration. One fellowship recipient will be selected by Mr. Elwes by calendar year's end.”

Deadline: November 1

Blacklist/NDRC Climate Storytelling Fellowship

Co-presented by The Blacklist and the National Resources Defense Council, this fellowship grants $20,000 each to three applicants every year. The award is intended to support the revision of a feature screenplay or pilot that engages with climate change in a compelling way.

Grantees will receive continued mentorship throughout the revision process, as well as access to relevant experts and consultants. Previous mentors include Brit Marling, Scott Z. Burns, and Mike Schur.

There is no fee to submit this application.

Deadline: December 4

Useful Links:

  • Documentary Grants - International Documentary Association
  • Funds For Writers - Opportunities for prose writers & screenwriters
  • Sundance Co//ab List of Opportunities - Sundance Institute
    (sign up for a free Co//ab account to see all grants)
  • Res Artis - Worldwide Network of Artist Residencies
  • Dear Producer - Opportunities and support guide for producers
Keep an eye on our Grants, Contests & Awards section, where we will be sharing new opportunities that come up throughout the season.

blogs.title: Ready for the New GoPro MISSION 1 PRO ILS? This Ultimate Creator Kit Is Already On Sale
blogs.description:
Just officially released the other day, the GoPro MISSION 1 PRO ILS is already one of the most intriguing new cameras of the year. It’s also one of the sneakier best-value cameras on the market, with the base model retailing at just under $700 here at launch. Yet if you want to fully power this promising compact cinema camera with its 8K30 and 4K120 Open Gate video, this Ultimate Creator Kit might be a good option.

It bumps the price a bit, but for a pretty reasonable price, you’ll get almost everything you need to use this new MISSION 1 PRO ILS as a fully functional cinema-camera workhorse. Let’s look at this new GoPro camera and explore this kit option.

The GoPro MISSION 1 PRO ILS


When first announced, the MISSION 1 PRO line from GoPro seemed like a stretch, or at least an ambitious move from the company best known for its rough-and-tumble action cameras. While the MISSION 1 PRO ILS has some action cam elements, it’s really a cinema camera packed into a compact form factor.

The camera itself features an MFT lens mount, a 50MP 1" image sensor, and a GP3 processor, which can easily capture up to 8K30 and 4K120 Open Gate video. The camera also promises strong low-light capture and a wide 14-stop dynamic range, which should make it efficient in any environment.

Plus, with a 159° field of view and enhanced zooming modes, shooters will be able to pretty much ensure that they won’t miss any of the action. You’ll also be able to swap between different Micro Four Thirds mount lenses for flexibility on set.

Kit Options


At launch, the GoPro MISSION 1 PRO ILS comes in a couple of kit editions, including a grip edition and a creator edition.

However, the real value for those looking to instantly level up their camera experience into a full rig build-out ready for on-the-run pro video production might be this Ultimate Creator Kit edition, which is set to feature the camera, a Hohem iSteady MT3 AI Camera Stabilizer, the GoPro Two-Person Wireless Mic Complete Kit, a GoPro Light Mod 2, and a GoPro Media Mod for MISSION 1 Series.

Pretty much everything one might need to unlock full video, sound, and stabilization for the camera. If you’re curious to explore this build-out, it’s out now and actually on sale. Here are the full specs and purchase options.

  • 50MP 1" Sensor & GP3 Processor
  • Media Mod, Light Mod 2
  • Fluid Pro AI Gimbal Stabilizer
  • 2-Person Wireless Mic System
  • Micro Four Thirds Lens Mount
  • 8K30 & 4K120 Open Gate (4:3) Capture
  • 8K60, 4K240 & 1080p960 Video Recording
  • HDR, 10-Bit, GP-Log2 & Timecode Sync
  • Enhanced Low-Light & Dynamic Range
  • 32-Bit Float Audio Recording

GoPro MISSION 1 PRO ILS Ultimate Creator Edition


The MISSION 1 PRO ILS Ultimate Creator Edition from GoPro equips you with the 8K compact cinema camera, a Media Mod, a Light Mod 2, a wireless mic system, and an AI-powered gimbal stabilizer. The camera boasts a compact size with an MFT lens mount. Use the gimbal to capture smooth footage and the mods to further improve audio and video quality.

blogs.title: 7Artisans Brings Another Bright Fisheye Lens With an Expansive 185° Angle of View to Filmmakers
blogs.description:
A new bright fisheye lens is now on the market for filmmakers, videographers, photographers, and hybrid content creators, offering something unique for its price point.

This new 10mm f/2.5 AF MAX Fisheye Lens from 7Artisans is set to feature an expansive and sweeping 185° angle of view and a bright f/2.5 maximum aperture, making it an intriguing option for those looking to capture wide shots for all types of action sports, vlogs, or other projects that require dynamic subject tracking.

Let’s check out what this new wide fisheye has to offer.

The 7Artisans 10mm f/2.5 AF MAX Fisheye Lens


Ideally a nice lens option for those looking for specific shots, and maybe not a true everyday walking-around type lens, this 7Artisans 10mm f/2.5 AF MAX Fisheye Lens will feature a 5.9" minimum focusing distance, which should help allow shooters to capture exaggerated perspectives, while a 9-blade diaphragm should also help to ensure smooth focus fall-off.

The lens should be a practical fisheye option, thanks in part to its autofocus, which should be useful for action sports, up-close events, vlog-style content, or any other applications that require dynamic subject tracking.

The lens should be quite lightweight too, coming in at just 1.1 lb, and it will also feature dual customizable function buttons to help with quick setting changes.

Price and Availability


Overall, another solid bright fisheye lens on the market for a diverse range of cameras and for a price point that’s pretty on par with its competition. Worth checking out if you want fisheye shots on your next project.

Here are the full specs and purchase options.

  • Full-Frame | f/2.5 to f/16
  • Fast Fisheye Lens with Autofocus
  • 5.9" Minimum Focus Distance
  • Clicked Aperture Ring
  • Customizable Function Button
  • 1 ASPH & 2 ED Elements
  • 9-Blade Diaphragm
  • USB-C Port for Firmware Upgrades

7Artisans 10mm f/2.5 AF MAX Fisheye Lens


The 10mm f/2.5 AF MAX Fisheye Lens from 7Artisans is a bright fisheye lens with a sweeping 185° angle of view and a bright f/2.5 maximum aperture. This fisheye lens is optimized for video in addition to still photography thanks to the incorporation of autofocus, making it simple to keep your subject in focus as they move.

blogs.title: Where Should Your Actor Look? Eyelines, Explained
blogs.description:
Eyelines are one of those invisible elements of filmmaking. When they work, you don't notice them at all. When they don't… whew, it's bad, and it's obvious.

If you have a scene where two characters are talking to each other, and suddenly one is looking in the wrong direction, or their gaze is off, even by a little, it's jarring. The scene falls apart because you're wondering what the heck they're looking at.

A new StudioBinder Academy video breaks down what eyelines are, how the 180-degree rule protects them, and how filmmakers like Kubrick, Spielberg, and Scorsese bend or break the rule intentionally.

Let's dive in.

- YouTube www.youtube.com

What Are Eyelines?

As StudioBinder says, "Eyelines are the backbone of continuity filmmaking."

Eyelines are simply where your actors are looking, specifically when they're looking off-screen at something that isn't in-frame with them. The audience needs to have some idea of what they're looking at, so they need to make sense.

If you have two characters in conversation, chances are they won't both be in the shot, especially if they're seated at a table or something similar.

This is where the 180-degree rule becomes so important. It protects the eyelines by keeping the camera on one side of an imaginary axis drawn between the two characters, so each character's gaze always points in a consistent direction through intercutting.

If you "break the plane" and this rule, say, by switching to the other side of the characters, you'll create a problem for yourself by having to track new eyelines. Plus it can make for a confusing edit and an uncomfortable watch for the audience.

The video gives The Shining as an example. When Jack meets the ghost in that iconic red bathroom, for the most part the camera sits on one side of the conversation. We get two-shots and singles, but we never cross the plane. The eyelines are continuous even when the coverage of the scene varies.

You'll want to make sure your eyelines make sense and are kept consistent. If one character is taller, for example, the other will need to look up. (This is one reason in special effects sequences, where one character might be a looming robot, for example, they'll wear a fake head to establish that eyeline. I'm thinking of K-2SO in Rogue One.)

- YouTube www.youtube.com

What To Do in Crowded Scenes

Here's a bit of advice, especially if you're an indie filmmaker. Try to limit the number of people in your scenes, for your own sanity. Not only does it make coverage more complicated, you likely have to mic all those people up, and sound can get expensive fast.

Anyway, I digress. What about eyelines here? What if you have a table scene with six or seven people sitting together?

The video offers these tips:

  1. Give the audience a clear establishing shot of the whole table. That way, they understand the geography of the scene and where everyone is sitting.
  2. Use two-shots and three-shots to maintain eyeline continuity.
  3. When you're breaking down your script or storyboarding, map out the table and where your 180-degree lines will go as the conversation progresses.

Spielberg is great at table scenes. Remember the tense discussion in Jurassic Park? What about the dinners in E.T.? Look to those and study them for strong examples of coverage in table scenes.

In Jurassic Park, the 180-degree lines change based on who jumps into the conversation at different points.

This only works because Spielberg's blocking is doing the lifting. If those characters were arranged differently around the table and we were just jumping around between them, the coverage would be super confusing.

Breaking the Plane (But Not the Audience)

If you have to break the 180-degree rule, and sometimes you do, there are ways to achieve it without confusing the audience.

Try using a cutaway shot between the two shots where you break the plane. This cutaway shouldn't be tied to the 180-degree line. It can be a "spatial reset" before you return to the conversation on the other side.

Continuous camera movement is the other way to do it. Famously, Quentin Tarantino likes to move the camera all the way around a group, and the video shows Reservoir Dogs as the example. If we're panning almost like our eyes would over different characters having their conversations, it feels natural enough to work. Our view isn't jumping around. That's what would be confusing, because we wouldn't know where we are.

Remember, only break the 180-degree rule when there's a reason for it. Don't do it just to "spice up" your coverage.

Are you trying to disorient your audience, which is the case in Martin Scorsese's Raging Bull? Are you approaching stories with a more formal, stylized shoot style, as was the case for Yasujiro Ozu? There are ways to break the rule, but you need to be prepared to justify your decision.

Eyelines as Storytelling

Your eyelines can serve as character work, too.

If Character A looks down at Character B, the eyeline can convey authority, threat, and size. If Character B looks up at Character A, then the eyeline suggests vulnerability, submission, or awe.

The same effect can be achieved by dropping or raising the camera on a single character, which makes the camera itself an eyeline participant.

Then you have POV shots. The camera becomes a character's eyeline, and the other characters are looking straight at us. (Don't confuse this with breaking the fourth wall. That's different.) This puts the audience in the character's shoes.

The video points to Ben Leonberg's Good Boy, a horror film told from a dog's perspective. Indy the dog's eyeline is only 19 inches off the ground, and the camera is consistently placed at that height throughout the film to maintain his perspective.

How to Prep for Eyelines

Again, read your script. Think about character dynamics in each scene. That will tell you where to place eyelines and your characters for blocking. Add eyelines to your shot lists. Storyboard. Give your actors marks so they know where to go in every take. Get a script supervisor to keep your eyelines straight.

Learning this will keep your filmmaking clean and consistent, and hopefully prevent you from making embarrassing eyeline mistakes.

blogs.title: You Can Now Run Eddie AI as an MCP Server, Unlocking Pay-As-You-Go Use for AI Assistant Editing
blogs.description:
The world of video editing keeps changing as the AI shakeup further shifts the bedrock of what we’ve known and held dear in digital video editing.

While the most intense, if not scary, developments in AI still have to do with generative AI models like Seedance, Kling, and others, the world of AI assistance is probably the best bet for those looking to take advantage of AI powers without fully succumbing to the full generative and replacement-type models.

If you’ve been curious about these AI assistance options, you’ve likely seen our coverage of tools like Eddie AI and others that offer chat-based assistance for pre-editing footage, pulling transcripts, soundbites, assembly, b-roll, captions, etc.

Eddie AI is now offering new ways to use its service with a pay-as-you-go model, which could be up to 50% more cost-efficient, along with new integrations and an iPhone app. Here’s what you need to know if you’re interested.

Eddie AI Pay-As-You-Go


The big news is that the company is now offering a pay-as-you-go model that lets users buy what they use, with no monthly fee to access the product. The assistant video editor app can also work directly from Claude or ChatGPT as an MCP server too, so anyone interested can cut their footage by talking to the assistant they already have open.

This should unlock around a hundred tools for those who might be into this type of thing, including transcripts, soundbites, assembly, b-roll, captions, music, voiceover, multicam angles, NLE export, and other features. All of these will be available inside ChatGPT, where the edit can come back as playable cards with real frames from your footage, not an external link.

Eddie AI iPhone App


The company has also released a native iPhone app on the App Store, giving video editors another option to work more directly with an AI assistant editor on their projects. The app uses a simple workflow: users can prompt an edit, watch the finished cut in a gapless player, save the MP4 to Photos, or share a link.

Footage can be imported directly from your camera roll, Drive, or Frame.io, and a push notification tells you when it is ready, so you can start the job and put the phone away. This app uses the same cloud projects as web and desktop, which live in the cloud and can sync live across web, desktop, and phone.

Plenty of Updates


Overall, Eddie AI has rolled out a lot in this space over the past few months, including generative sound and b-roll, as well as its own AI video editing model, EddieEditor1-9B. Eddie AI isn’t the only company working in this space; other assistant video editor apps are launching, and similar offerings are being built into Premiere, but with a wide range of tools, it’s certainly one of the most expansive options right now.

If you’d like to find out more, the company shares that it will be at IBC2026 at RAI Amsterdam, 11–14 September at Hall 7, stand 7.A38 — the main booth, live demos throughout the show — and Hall 14, Future Tech pod 14.B51, in the AI zone.

You can find more info on the company’s website here.

blogs.title: How a Wine-Infused Cold Email & Pool Parties Got 'Pools' Noticed
blogs.description:
In this episode of the No Film School Podcast, Writer-director Sam Hayes and actor-filmmaker Michael Vlamis break down the making and unconventional release of Pools, a coming-of-age film built around an overnight pool-hopping adventure.

They discuss the logistical challenges of shooting underwater on an indie schedule, building an ensemble cast around specific actors, and why traditional distribution offers pushed the team toward a hands-on grassroots strategy. Sam explains how pool-party premieres, years of networking, and a wine-fueled cold email helped Pools find a new audience through the Letterboxd Video Store, while Michael compares the scrappy production of Pools with working on Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey.

They also share lessons on preserving release momentum, budgeting for marketing, navigating film festivals, and finding an audience when streamers are not an option.


In this episode, we discuss:

  • How the image of a glowing pool at night became the foundation for Pools
  • Writing characters with specific actors like Michael Vlamis, Odessa A'zion, and Tyler Alvarez in mind
  • Building chemistry within an ensemble cast on a limited indie prep schedule
  • The complications of filming overnight pool scenes and shooting underwater
  • How a breath coach helped Odessa A'zion increase her underwater breath hold from roughly 15 seconds to a minute and a half
  • Why Sam turned down disappointing traditional distribution offers and pursued a more hands-on service deal
  • Creating pool-party premieres that made screenings feel like events rather than another movie release
  • How Sam became a top 0.01% Partiful user while organizing approximately 25 promotional events
  • Why filmmakers need to actively build relationships with festival programmers, distributors, critics, and other members of the indie film community
  • The mistake of delaying Pools' TVOD release in hopes of benefiting from the attention around Odessa A'zion's other projects
  • Why maintaining momentum and giving audiences an immediate way to watch a film matters after theatrical release
  • How the crowded TVOD marketplace makes discoverability especially difficult for independent movies
  • The wine-fueled cold email Sam wrote to Letterboxd after feeling like the film was running out of distribution options
  • Why Letterboxd's curated Video Store offered Pools a way to stand apart from algorithm-driven platforms
  • How the film's Letterboxd rating improved as more viewers discovered it
  • Michael's experience moving between Pools, his indie feature Crossword, and Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey
  • Why a giant production can still feel surprisingly scrappy and responsive on set
  • The difference between a film's production budget and the marketing budget needed to actually break through
  • Why indie filmmakers cannot build their entire distribution strategy around getting acquired by a major streamer
  • How real-world relationships can turn previous distribution passes into new opportunities
  • Why Sam recommends budgeting for marketing before production begins
  • The danger of submitting a rough cut to major film festivals before the movie is truly ready
  • Michael's approach to finding grounded comedy without forcing jokes or overthinking a performance

blogs.title: Inside 25 Years of Tribeca: What Independent Filmmakers Need to Know
blogs.description:
In this episode of the No Film School Podcast, Tribeca Festival Director and SVP of Programming Cara Cusumano joins host GG Hawkins to reflect on 25 years of Tribeca and explain what independent filmmakers should understand about today’s festival landscape.

Cusumano discusses Tribeca’s evolution from its post-9/11 roots into a multidisciplinary storytelling festival, how programmers evaluate nearly 14,000 submissions, why filmmakers should build relationships with their peers instead of chasing gatekeepers, and how festivals are responding to shifts in film distribution and audience behavior.

She also shares how emerging filmmakers can participate in festival communities even without a film in the lineup and why creating distinctive work matters more than waiting for the perfect opportunity.


In this episode, we discuss:

  • How Tribeca’s founding mission of community, connection, and celebrating movies has endured across 25 years
  • Cara’s path from attending the first Tribeca Festival as a film student to becoming Festival Director and SVP of Programming
  • Why networking is really about building relationships with your contemporaries and growing together throughout your careers
  • How programmers view filmmakers and why they are actively looking for work to champion rather than trying to keep filmmakers out
  • What makes a project feel distinctly right for Tribeca, from independent storytelling to memorable audience experiences
  • How Tribeca manages and evaluates nearly 14,000 film and project submissions
  • Why passionate advocacy inside the programming room can matter even when programmers disagree about a film
  • Why festival feedback is complicated and how programming decisions can depend on the composition of the entire lineup, not simply the quality of an individual film
  • How Tribeca expanded beyond features and shorts into television, podcasts, games, VR, immersive work, and creator-driven storytelling
  • The value of human curation as an alternative to algorithmic discovery
  • Why Tribeca is interested in projects that blur the boundaries between film, games, immersive media, podcasts, and other formats
  • How the role of film festivals is changing as selling an independent film directly out of a festival becomes more difficult
  • Why festivals increasingly function as places for talent discovery, career building, networking, and demonstrating audience demand
  • How the in-person festival experience can create moments that cannot be replicated through individual at-home viewing
  • How emerging filmmakers can participate in Tribeca through programs like the Storytelling Summit even if their work is not selected
  • Why Cara hopes Tribeca remains flexible enough to respond to new forms of storytelling that do not yet have an established industry category
  • Her advice to stop waiting for the perfect moment, keep collaborating, and make work because of the story rather than its potential festival or distribution outcome

blogs.title: The Uncanny Power of Famous Actors' Final On-Screen Lines
blogs.description:
I love movies so much, mostly because you never know what magic you're going to get on screen. From the real, accidental dolphins in The Odyssey to the shooting stars you can see in Jaws, when you run a camera, you never know what you're going to get.

Sometimes, it's the final words of someone famous on screen.

Whether by sheer coincidence or an intentional meta-narrative, legendary performers often have their final words to the public play out on screen.

Today, I want to look at a few that I find to be quite powerful.

Let's dive in.

Actors' last scenes ever www.youtube.com

1. Robin Williams — Night at the Museum: Secret of the Tomb (2014)

"Smile, my boy. It's sunrise."

Damn, that made me cry. I loved Robin Williams so much. He was an inspiration to me and to many of my friends in comedy.

Robin Williams brought immeasurable warmth to his performance as Teddy Roosevelt throughout the Night at the Museum trilogy that sort of made you believe he would be around forever.

In his final live-action role, we hear these words before his character reverts to a wax figure as the morning light breaks over the museum.

It's an awesome reminder to see the best in every situation and to look forward to new days.

2. Val Kilmer — Top Gun: Maverick (2022)

"One last thing... Who's the better pilot? You or me?"

Val Kilmer’s return as Tom "Iceman" Kazansky was one of the most emotional highlights of Top Gun: Maverick.

I saw this movie on opening night, and you could hear people crying during this scene.

And yes, one of them was me.

The poignant connection of these two men with the meta-revelation of their roles was so special.

This final humorous line breaks the tension of the scene and brings joy back ot he forefrotn. The brotherhood and ball-busting show that nothing changes, even as sickness takes everything else from us.

3. Oliver Reed — Gladiator (2000)

"Shadows and dust."

The legends of Oliver Reed during the shooting of Gladiator are numerous. From outdrinking military members to antagonizing castmates, he was larger than life.

The famed actor passed away during the production of Ridley Scott’s Gladiator, so the filmmakers had to use early CGI, body doubles, and reallocated footage to complete his performance as Proximo.

Still, they picked the best parting lines for him that cinema could ask for.

In the scene, Proximo reminds Maximus of mortality and the fleeting nature of glory. His recurring line caps off a career defined by being a one-of-a-kind rogue.

4. Kevin Conroy — Justice League x RWBY: Super Heroes & Huntsmen (2023)

"If it has to end, at least I go out like this... Being Batman!"

Who is the best Batman of all time? Well, I think it's Kevin Conroy.

For over thirty years, Conroy was the definitive voice of Batman for generations of fans who grew up on Batman: The Animated Series and the Arkham video game series.

To this day, I still hear his voice when I see images from those shows.

In one of his final voice performances, Conroy's Dark Knight delivers a defiant line that reads like a thesis statement for his entire career. And one fitting goodbye to an icon whose voice will be missed, but will go on forever.

5. Robert Redford — Dark Winds (2025)

"George... the whole world is waiting. Make a move."

While Redford had retired from feature films after The Old Man & the Gun, his true final on-screen appearance before his passing came in a 30-second television cameo alongside George R.R. Martin in the TV show Dark Winds.

It's a wild scene where he is sitting across a chessboard from the Game of Thrones author. You have this meta joke on waiting for the book, and also a lighthearted quip from one storyteller to another about wondering what comes next.

6. Tony Todd — Final Destination: Bloodlines (2025)

"Life is precious. Enjoy every single second. You never know when... Good luck."

Tony Todd’s deep, ominous voice made him a titan of the horror genre. He had many awesome roles, but I loved him as the mysterious mortician William Bludworth across the Final Destination franchise.

Before his passing in late 2024, Todd filmed a final appearance for Final Destination: Bloodlines to offer background on his iconic character and a line that was so fitting, it's the perfect way to end.

That kind of gratitude in a movie about dying is awesome and added another layer to one of the best Final Destination movies.

Summing It All Up

These were some emotional clips, but I hope they gave you a kick in the pants to make sure the words you put on paper mean something. You never know when someone famous will pass and you'll have their last words on screen, so put effort and care into your writing.

You never know what's next.

Let me know what you think in the comments.

blogs.title: Meet the Artists Behind the Emmy-Nominated VFX on Gen V
blogs.description:
Set in the Emmy-winning world of The Boys, Gen V superheroes are still learning to control their powers, and the results can get messy. For VFX Supervisor Karen Heston and VFX Producer Sean Tompkins, bringing that chaos to life meant grounding even the most outrageous moments in reality, blending physical performances and practical effects with seamless digital work.

Working alongside artists at DNEG, Heston and Tompkins carried that approach across hundreds of shots, from detailed characters and environments to the show’s signature gore. With as many as eight episodes and 1400 shots moving through post at once, the team relied on Adobe Substance, Adobe Premiere, and Adobe Photoshop to collaborate across departments and tackle complex VFX challenges. For some of the show’s most gruesome moments, artists used body-tracked digital doubles to simulate blood, organs, bones, and explosions—giving the team precise control while keeping the action rooted in the actors’ performances.

Heston, Tompkins, and the team at DNEG—VFX Producer Oliver Eikhoff and VFX Supervisors Andrew Simmonds and Bhanu Prakash—sat down with us to discuss the power of thoughtful world-building and their love of well-executed gore.

Karen, as VFX Supervisor, what was the overall creative vision for the VFX on Gen V? How did you work with DNEG to bring that vision to life?

Karen Heston: Our overall creative vision for the VFX on Gen V was to make everything feel as grounded and visceral as possible, even when the story became completely insane. We wanted the audience to believe these characters and their powers existed in a real world—with real physical consequences—rather than feeling like they were simply watching a superhero show.

A big part of that was finding the balance between practical effects and VFX. We always wanted the performances, camera, lighting, and physicality of the actors to drive the shot. VFX was there to enhance that reality and take it somewhere we couldn't achieve practically, not replace it.

I’ve worked with DNEG’s Oliver Eikhoff for a long time, and I was thrilled when he came on board for Gen V. Likewise, Andrew Simmonds is DNEG’s VFX Supervisor, and that role really requires being in sync, not only creatively, but technically. You need to have a shared aesthetic and a common understanding of how to execute the vision. They bring incredible technical knowledge while always understanding the bigger creative picture, which makes collaboration easy.

Together, we were able to build a really strong relationship between production and DNEG, and work as one team to carry the creative vision of Gen V through every stage of the process.

Oliver, as DNEG’s VFX Producer, what was the collaboration like with Karen, Sean and the broader Gen V VFX team?

Oliver Eikhoff: The collaboration was fantastic! We already worked together on the first season of Gen V and had established a great working relationship. For season 2, we got involved relatively early while the shoot was still going on. This helped us a lot with the planning and casting of our internal team of artists to make sure everything was aligned for the much bigger scale of this season.

The communication with Karen and Sean was what I would say stood out the most: it really felt like we were collaborating and working together to help realize the creative vision of the show.

Episodic productions are incredibly fast-paced: at one point we were working on all eight episodes simultaneously while developing multiple hero effects across our total of 450 shots. Thanks to Karen's and Sean's strong leadership and clear communication, we were consistently working toward our common goal of delivering the high-quality standard expected for a show set in the Vought Cinematic Universe.

Sean, as VFX Producer, what did your role look like across the project from initial planning through final delivery?

Sean Tompkins: The road on Gen V was quite a long one. For this project, VFX ends up on the project for about 1.5 years from start to finish. My process starts with an initial breakdown of the script, where I highlight and call out any possible visual effects. From there, I create a VFX breakdown and confer with Karen to make sure we are on the same page with the callouts. I then move into a first pass of numbers where we are also putting together the initial shot count estimates for the episode to help gauge the budget.

Once production starts, I work with Karen to make sure that the numbers we initially talked about with everyone are what is shot and that nothing is added. I also watch dailies to make sure we stay on track, and there are not “gotchas” looming out there to surprise us.

When production wraps for an episode, we are quickly into post. As soon as I can get my hands on a cut, I start to put together some initial budgets and flag anything that is largely outside of our original VFX scope. Once we get closer to locked cuts, we start to share with the vendors to get a sense of where they are really landing and to put together our final vendor work plan. On Gen V, we were able to get our turnovers started at the Studio cut phase, so at that point we get started on shot work. The shot work period is a roughly 6-month roller coaster of notes, schedules, and potential overages that we navigate across 1400 shots and hope to end up right on pattern and on schedule at the end.

What Adobe tools did the DNEG team use throughout the project, and what made them the right fit for the work?

OE: At DNEG, Photoshop is a staple across multiple departments. Our concept art team leans heavily on it to design key looks, such as Jordan’s vein look and the Elmira prison environment, before we get to CG. From there, Photoshop is our go-to for matte painting. On Gen V, we used it for everything from bathroom mirror smudges in Episode 201 to blood on the seminar room floor in Episode 208.

Substance 3D Painter is a core component of our texturing pipeline, used heavily by our build and environment teams. The software allows us to rapidly look-dev and apply complex textures to our assets. Additionally, Premiere served as the primary editorial tool for Gen V at DNEG, playing an essential role in organizing the shot lineup and ensuring seamless alignment with the production team. Our typical turnover workflow begins by importing the sequence cut and pull EDL into Premiere to establish a master timeline. We also used Premiere for QC; each version is imported and cut into the timeline to verify that frame ranges, color, and overall framing match the provided editorial reference before updates are shared with the production team.

Andrew and Bhanu, as DNEG’s VFX Supervisors, what were some of the biggest creative or technical challenges you encountered, and how did you solve them?

Bhanu Prakash: We had a bunch of complex challenges to tackle across multiple sequences, but the one that immediately comes to mind is the Godolkin skin-healing sequence in Episode 207. We had to visually show Godolkin’s grotesque skin gradually transforming back to normal skin. To achieve this, we had to model two variations of Godolkin, one with the grotesque skin and another with the regular skin. We then did body tracking for each shot, after which FX simulated the skin transition in patches. The simulated maps were then provided to lighting, who rendered both variations. These were finally brought together and revealed in comp to achieve the final look.

Andrew Simmonds: Another creative challenge was working on the Godolkin explosion moment from Episode 208. Using our FX team to tear flesh and simulate blood and gore was complex. We started building our high-resolution Godolkin digital double. This included skin, muscles, internal organs, and a skeleton. We then worked out the best way to explode the character by body-tracking the plate and then doing a digital takeover of our CG asset, with the animation driving the FX simulation to throw the blood and gore where we wanted. Once we had this, we systematically went through each layer and tuned it until we were happy with its performance.

'Gen V'Image Courtesy of Amazon MGM Studios | Gen V

Image Courtesy of Amazon MGM Studios | Gen V

What was your favorite VFX sequence, shot, or element from the project? How did it come together, and what went into achieving the final result?

KH: One of my favorite elements was the evolution of Marie’s blood powers, particularly the tendrils. We never wanted them to feel like red energy beams; they needed to retain the weight, viscosity, translucency, and unpredictability of real blood.

We built the effect around Jaz Sinclair's performance and choreography developed by John Koyama, using practical blood, prosthetics, and interactive elements wherever possible. DNEG then extended that work digitally, refining the movement, lighting, droplets, and contact with Marie and her environment. It’s a great example of what Gen V does best: combining character, performance, practical effects, and complex digital work without allowing the spectacle to overwhelm the story.

ST: My favorite sequence in the season was Tiny Emma running through the fraternity. I loved the amount of prep and thought that went into this sequence. We started with some initial talks with the Director and Executive Producers about the basic beats and flow of the sequence. In order to really sell the fact that Emma was tiny, we knew we were going to need to ground her in the tiny world through intentional prop placement and scaling.

In our tech viz stage, we calculated the size the lamp base or floor tiles would need to be and laid out the blue screen based on the size Emma had shrunk down to. The practical camera lensing needed to translate Emma from her blue screen practical size into the practical background plates of the partygoers' feet. After all plates had been shot, we enlisted the team at DNEG to help us put the shots together. With DNEG, we worked to make sure the focus levels were right to properly set her depth of field. We also added some atmospheric elements and some animated CG pieces, like the bouncing cigarette, to really sell the world of Tiny Emma.

BK: My favorite sequence would be the blood bag. To achieve the desired look, we had to go through multiple iterations involving Asset, Animation, FX, and CFX. Once we got the desired movement and overall look, the next challenge was balancing the air movement inside the bag and the blood residue at the top to match the practical effects as closely as possible.

Watch Gen V on Amazon Prime Video.
